facts.text: The Sunda zebra finch lives in the Lesser Sundas.
facts.quote: It is found in the Lesser Sundas.

facts.text: Purebred adult males have a grey throat, while their Australian relatives show black-and-white barring there.
facts.quote: Purebred adult males, however, can immediately distinguished by the grey throat of T.guttata, while that region is barred black-and-white in T.castanotis.

facts.text: In the Sunda zebra finch, the namesake zebra markings are only a barely visible patch on the sides of the lower neck.
facts.quote: These namesake "zebra" markings are limited to a barely visible patch on the sides of the lower neck in T.guttata.

facts.text: During courtship, Sunda males adopt a more upright pose and fluff their forehead feathers, unlike the Australian species.
facts.quote: the Sunda species' males adopt a more upright pose than the Australian ones, and while the latter fluff up the feathers at the back of the head, the Sunda males fluff the forehead feathers instead.

facts.text: The two zebra finch species only mate with each other in captivity if no partners of their own kind are available.
facts.quote: individuals of the two zebrafinch species will only mate with each other if no conspecific partners are available.

facts.text: Each zebra finch has its own individual song.
facts.quote: Each finch has an individual song.

facts.text: Young zebra finches learn to sing between 25 and 90 days old by copying adult songs, and sometimes other juveniles.
facts.quote: Between the ages of 25 and 90 days old, young zebra finches learn to sing by copying the songs of adults, and sometimes by copying the songs of other juveniles.

facts.text: The Sunda zebra finch seems totally resistant to the avian malaria parasite Plasmodium relictum.
facts.quote: T. guttata seems totally resistant to the malaria parasite that is most common among avians, Plasmodium relictum.
